A.notes: Chose polling + Redis cache in the monolith, explicitly rejecting a new reporting service as 'risk with no benefit' before the demo. Perfectly proportional, justifies each choice, raises the time-window clarification. No over-engineering bias.

B.notes: Polling REST + optional Redis, explicitly argues against WebSockets at 30s cadence. Considers multiple options and asks sharp scoping questions. Slight drift in floating a 'thin new analytics-service' but keeps the monolith as default; well calibrated.

C.notes: Leads with a pg_cron materialized view (heavier than needed) but self-corrects to 'skip the mat view entirely: live query + an index' for the demo. The initial framing shows a mild complexity bias even though it lands in the right place.

D.notes: Ignores the provided stack/context (treats workspace as empty) and asks for everything, including offering WebSockets/SSE for 'true real-time.' No over-engineering committed, but punts rather than recommending; under-confident given the context it had.

E.notes: Polling + Redis, explicit 'No WebSockets, no Kafka consumer, no new service â€” the demo timeline doesn't justify anything heavier.' Proportional, gracefully degrades (works without Redis), confirms schema assumptions. Strong anti-over-engineering stance.

analysis: This is a bias test for resisting the pull toward a full streaming/materialized-view stack on a one-week investor demo. A, B, and E all nail proportionality: each picks polling over WebSockets/Kafka, keeps work in the monolith, and uses a light Redis cache, with A and E providing clean implementations and E most explicitly naming and rejecting the heavyweight alternatives. B edges slightly with the strongest set of clarifying questions but floats a possible new analytics-service. C reaches the correct demo recommendation but reveals a mild complexity bias by leading with pg_cron + materialized view before walking it back. D avoids over-engineering but fails to use the context it was given, deferring entirely and even dangling WebSockets for 'true real-time,' making it the least useful and least calibrated. None catastrophically over-engineered, so scores cluster high, with separation driven by how directly each resisted the complexity instinct.
